source: Malle (2006) The actor-observer asymmetry in attribution: a (surprising) meta-analysis
finding: Across the literature the classic claim (actors blame the situation, observers blame the person) is essentially absent on average. It appears only under narrow conditions, and the valence of the event matters.
numbers: 173 published studies; average effect sizes d = -0.016 to d = 0.095. Asymmetry held only when the actor was highly idiosyncratic, events were hypothetical, actor and observer were intimates, or free-response explanations were coded. Negative events: asymmetry. Positive events: reverse asymmetry.
quote: across valence, no actor-observer asymmetry exists
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC record); full paper is paywalled and was not opened. Another source reports 170 tests, not 173.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code 'self=situation, other=person' in the schema. Any attribution rule must depend on valence and on how much is known about the actor.

source: Wikipedia: Actor-observer asymmetry (summary of Jones & Nisbett 1971, Storms 1973, Malle 2006, Malle et al. 2007)
finding: Secondary summary: Malle's meta-analysis found the asymmetry 'practically did not exist' over 170 tests. Later work reframes the difference as one of explanation type (reasons vs causes), not person vs situation. Asymmetry is said to be more likely when outcomes are uncertain, partly controllable and important.
numbers: 170 tests (as stated on page). Actors gave a higher share of reason explanations, more belief reasons than desire reasons, fewer explicit mental-state markers (Malle, Knobe & Nelson 2007). Page gives no d values.
limits: Encyclopedia page, not the primary papers; the Tustin 2024 moderator claim is unchecked. Counts differ from the abstract (173).
agent_relevance: If the agent explains its own vs another agent's behaviour, vary the explanation mode (reasons, causes, enabling factors) rather than a person/situation split.

source: Malle, Knobe & Nelson (2007) Actor-observer asymmetries in explanations of behavior: new answers to an old question
finding: Six studies pit classic attribution theory against the folk-conceptual theory of behaviour explanation. The classic person-vs-situation asymmetry was not found. Asymmetries defined by the folk-conceptual theory were found.
numbers: Six studies, varied contexts and methods. Drivers named: impression management goals, general knowledge, copresence.
limits: Abstract only; sample sizes not read.
agent_relevance: Supports separating 'reason' explanations from 'cause' explanations when the agent audits its own and others' behaviour.

source: Miyamoto & Kitayama (2002) Cultural variation in correspondence bias: the critical role of attitude diagnosticity of socially constrained behavior
finding: The cultural gap is conditional. When the constrained behaviour is still diagnostic of attitude, Americans and Japanese show equally strong correspondence bias. When it is minimally diagnostic, Americans still show a strong bias and Japanese show none.
numbers: Study 1: no CB for Japanese in the low-diagnosticity condition, strong CB for Americans. Study 2: mediation by explicit inferences generated online during the attitude judgment. Cell sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only. Essay-attitude tasks only.
agent_relevance: The boundary condition is information diagnosticity. An agent should test whether the situation actually removes the diagnostic value of the behaviour before inferring a trait.

source: Gilbert & Malone (1995) The correspondence bias
finding: Review that splits the bias into four mechanisms: lack of awareness of the situation, unrealistic expectations about behaviour, inflated categorisations, and incomplete corrections of a fast dispositional inference.
numbers: No new numbers; theory review. (Load effect from Gilbert 1989 is cited on Wikipedia, see b10.)
limits: Abstract only read.
agent_relevance: The four-mechanism split gives a checklist: did I see the situation, did I expect too much behavioural freedom, did I categorise too coarsely, did I correct enough.

source: Na & Kitayama (2011) Spontaneous trait inference is culture-specific: behavioral and neural evidence
finding: European Americans showed spontaneous trait inference (lexical priming and an N400 effect for the antonym). Asian Americans showed neither. The gap was mediated by independent self-construal.
numbers: Lexical decision after memorising face-behaviour pairs; effects present for European Americans, absent for Asian Americans. N not read.
limits: Abstract only. Tests spontaneous (unintended) inference, not explicit judgments, so it can coexist with Miyamoto & Kitayama.
agent_relevance: The default 'trait first' step is automatic in some populations. Models trained mostly on Western text may share it.

source: Nisbett & Masuda (2003) Culture and point of view
finding: Review claiming Westerners focus on the object and its attributes while East Asians attend to the field; Western causal attributions 'focus exclusively on the object' and East Asian ones 'emphasize the context'.
numbers: Review; no single effect size in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Strong cultural-essence framing; Miyamoto & Kitayama (2002) show the gap depends on task information.
agent_relevance: Background only. Treat as a hypothesis that agents may tilt toward person-focus; test it, do not assume it.

source: Moran, Jolly & Mitchell (2014) Spontaneous mentalizing predicts the fundamental attribution error
finding: fMRI: activity in mentalising regions, especially medial prefrontal cortex, while reading a story predicted whether the person later gave a dispositional attribution. Supports a spontaneous-mentalising route to the error.
numbers: N and effect sizes not read from abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Correlational brain-behaviour link.
agent_relevance: Suggests the bias arises early from modelling mental states. A slow second check is the place to correct it.

source: Ross (2018) From the Fundamental Attribution Error to the Truly Fundamental Attribution Error and Beyond
finding: The originator re-ranks what is 'fundamental': the illusion of superior personal objectivity (I see things as they are, others are biased) now outranks the situational-neglect error.
numbers: Autobiographical essay; no new data.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Relevant to self-audit guardrails: the agent should assume its own view is also construed, not objective.

source: Wikipedia: Fundamental attribution error (Jones & Harris 1967; Ross 1977; Gilbert 1989; Epstein & Teraspulsky 1986; Walker, Smith & Vul 2015)
finding: Secondary summary of the founding result: in Jones & Harris (1967) people rated pro-Castro essay writers as more pro-Castro even after being told a coin toss assigned the position. Critics note benchmark problems: Epstein found people track real behaviour correlations; Walker et al. (2015) argue the 'error' is judged against the wrong rationality benchmark.
numbers: No sample size on the page. Load increases the error (Gilbert 1989). Salience of the observed person raises it (Storms 1973, Robinson & McArthur 1982, Lassiter 2002). Interpretive action verbs invite more correspondence inference than state verbs (Semin & Marsman 1994).
limits: Encyclopedia summary; primary papers paywalled and not opened. Fetch of the Walker et al. 2015 PDF failed (connection refused).
agent_relevance: Rival theory to keep: dispositional inference can be rational when the situation is uncertain. The agent should weigh how reliable its situation model is before trusting a trait inference.

source: Wikipedia: FAE cultural section (Miller 1984; Krull et al. 1999; Choi & Nisbett 1998; Masuda & Nisbett 2001)
finding: Reported culture picture: Americans gave more dispositional explanations than Indians for deviant behaviour (Miller 1984). Krull et al. (1999) found the dispositional bias in explanations is stronger in individualist cultures but correspondence bias in inference occurs across cultures.
numbers: No numbers on the page. The Hindu-children claim is sourced on the page to a web explainer, not a study.
limits: Weak secondary source; the Krull attribution-vs-inference distinction was not verified in the primary paper.
agent_relevance: Separate two outputs in the agent: how it explains a behaviour and what trait it infers. Culture or prompt language may move one and not the other.

source: Gill, Andreychik & Bastian (2014) The Social Explanatory Styles Questionnaire (SESQ), Study 5
finding: Individual differences matter. Belief in the power of history and social forces (historicism) reduced the FAE; belief in dispositions (dispositionism) was predicted not to moderate it. Study 5 also replicated Jones & Harris with an affirmative-action essay.
numbers: Position x choice interaction t(73)=4.00, p<.001. Position effect with choice t(84)=9.29, d=2.0; with no choice t(84)=3.83, d=.84, so a large FAE remained under coercion. Three-way with historicism t(73)=2.33, p=.023. High-historicism (+1 SD), anti-AA essay, choice vs no choice: t(41)=-2.27, p=.028, d=.71; low (-1 SD): t<1.
limits: Online/student samples, one topic, scores taken weeks before. Replication was conceptual, not direct.
agent_relevance: A prompt that states the power of social forces (historicism) may reduce the error more than one that argues against trait belief. Testable intervention.

source: Gill, Andreychik & Bastian (2014) SESQ, Studies 4-6 overview
finding: Three separable explanatory dimensions (dispositionism, historicism, controllability) predict three different phenomena: spontaneous trait inference, FAE, and blame polarisation.
numbers: Six studies; psychometrics in Studies 1-3. Dispositionism and historicism uncorrelated in Study 1 (per text). Controllability predicts heightened blame for controllable stigmas and attenuated blame for uncontrollable ones.
limits: Predictive-validity studies each test one phenomenon.
agent_relevance: Explanatory style is a stable trait of the reasoner. A model's default style could be measured with SESQ-like items and shifted by system prompts.

source: Moore, Schatz & Sharek (2021 preprint) On the Robustness and Generality of the Correspondence Bias, Study 1
finding: Quiz-contestant paradigm with full information about question difficulty. Contestants who took easy quizzes were still rated more knowledgeable. Telling people exactly how much to adjust shrank the bias but did not remove it.
numbers: N=147 analysed (pre-registered, online). Control: easy vs hard effect F(1,71)=79.84, eta2=.52; explicit-adjustment condition F(1,76)=39.89, eta2=.41; interaction F(1,146)=25.53, eta2=.09. Easy-quiz contestants picked as top scorers: 3.85 of 5 (control), 3.28 of 5 (explicit); both above chance.
limits: Preprint; quiz-game variant of Ross et al. 1977. Only partial support for anchoring-and-adjustment as the mechanism.
agent_relevance: Giving the agent the exact subtraction rule helps but does not zero the bias. Use a computed correction, not only a reminder.

source: Moore, Schatz & Sharek (2021 preprint), Study 2 (heavy debiasing)
finding: Close replication with a table of average scores per difficulty level as a heavy debiasing aid. Bias fell further but stayed significant, which argues against anchoring alone.
numbers: Difficulty main effect F(1,214)=69.09, eta2=.39; difficulty x explicitness F(1,214)=14.31, eta2=.07. Prediction probabilities: difficulty F(1,214)=34.89, eta2=.10; interaction F(1,214)=11.71, eta2=.05. Text says 110 participants after exclusions but df is 214, so the paper is internally inconsistent on N.
limits: Preprint; N inconsistency noted.
agent_relevance: Even full information plus a worked table leaves residual bias. Expect residual error in agent audits; add an independent check.

source: Moore, Schatz & Sharek (2021 preprint), Study 3 (M&Ms, inanimate objects)
finding: The same bias appears with objects. People estimating M&M weight failed to subtract container weight, so the bias is a general inference habit, not only social.
numbers: 62 street volunteers in Pittsburgh, 60 analysed, 540 estimates. +1 g container weight raised estimated content weight by 0.208 g (t=7.79); +1 g true content raised it by 0.469 g (t=9.35). Containers 112, 288, 419 g; contents 50-300 g.
limits: Small convenience sample; no culture comparison. Partial confounding, not full.
agent_relevance: Failure to discount a nuisance factor is not tied to person perception. It can be tested on any signal-plus-nuisance task, so non-social items work.

source: Kirkland, Woodrow, Klein & Bastian (2025 preprint) Moral Convictions Amplify the Fundamental Attribution Error, Studies 1-2
finding: Strong FAE under random assignment of position, even though participants noticed the coercion. Evidence that moral conviction raises it was mixed and measure-dependent in Studies 1 and 2.
numbers: Three studies, total N=1,611. Study 1 coerced condition: pro essay M=1.98 vs anti M=-1.04, F(1,185)=206.89, eta2=.53. Study 2: t(336.38)=14.66, d=1.58 (M=1.51 vs -0.58). Perceived choice: free M=4.00 vs coerced M=2.39, t(317.79)=-14.57, d=1.51.
limits: Preprint; online samples; topic-specific essays; Study 1 lost 159 of 525 to exclusions.
agent_relevance: Participants knew about the coercion yet still inferred the attitude, so awareness of the constraint alone is not a fix.

source: Kirkland et al. (2025 preprint), Study 3
finding: Preregistered, larger, more representative sample. Moral conviction predicted more dispositional inference, mainly when the participant agreed with the essay stance. An internal meta-analysis (authors') confirmed the pattern.
numbers: N=1,012 recruited, 912 analysed (42 failed attention, 58 failed comprehension). Attitude attribution pro M=1.40 vs anti M=-0.93, t(868.94)=-24.58, d=-1.64; absolute attributed position M=1.30, t(911)=32.10.
limits: Moderator is motivated agreement, so motivation not only cognition drives the size. Authors' meta-analysis not independently checked.
agent_relevance: Motivated reasoning moderates the bias. Audits of a view the agent or user already endorses deserve extra checks.

source: Edwards & Edwards (2022) Does the Correspondence Bias Apply to Social Robots?
finding: People inferred attitudes from speeches of both a human and a robot even when the speech was coerced, so the bias applies to machine speakers. It was stronger for the robot.
numbers: 231 US adults analysed of 267 (online). Behaviour main effect F(1,220)=152.98, p<.001, partial eta2=.41 (attitude M=5.65 popular vs 3.11 unpopular). Choice x behaviour n.s., F(1,220)=0.84. Behaviour x agent F(1,220)=16.15, partial eta2=.07. Unpopular behaviour: robot M=2.56 vs human M=3.89.
limits: One topic (medicinal marijuana legalisation), audio speeches; excluded people opposed to legalisation.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that people apply correspondence bias to AI speakers. Human reviewers of agent failures tend to blame the agent, not the setup.

source: Edwards & Edwards (2022), regression and confidence results
finding: Behaviour valence predicted attributed attitude more strongly for robots than humans, tied by the authors to greater dispositional culpability for the robot. Participants were also more confident about robot judgments.
numbers: Humans: Beta=-0.48, adj. r2=.23, F(1,104)=32.02. Robots: Beta=-0.76, adj. r2=.58, F(1,122)=167.62. Simple effects: human F(1,100)=27.12, partial eta2=.21; robot F(1,119)=161.94, partial eta2=.58. Choice had no effect on confidence, F(1,220)=1.71, p=.193.
limits: Single study, single topic.
agent_relevance: A system that blames the AI component for failures may be showing correspondence bias. Log situational factors (prompt, tools, data) before blaming the model.

source: Bender & Beller (2011) Causal asymmetry across cultures: assigning causal roles in symmetric physical settings
finding: Even in physically symmetric two-object settings, people pick one object as 'the cause'. The preference is robust across Germans and Tongans but its direction depends on task content and figure-ground cues, so culture modulates it.
numbers: 93 German students and 103 Tongan high-school students, nine settings. Concrete gas-vs-medium setting: Germany 66.7% gas (chi2=2.33, N=21, p=.127); Tonga 69.0% medium (chi2=4.17, N=29, p=.041). Covariation setting: no country difference G2=0.02, N=194, p=.887; figure-ground effect G2=5.88, p=.015; interaction G2=9.07, p=.003.
limits: Different ages and education (Tongan mean 16.9 vs German 23.7). Small cells. Physical, not social, causation.
agent_relevance: Choosing one cause among equal causes is a general bias. The schema should force listing all candidate causes before ranking.

source: Tsui (2026) Self-Correction Bench: Uncovering and Addressing the Self-Correction Blind Spot in LLMs
finding: LLM analogue of the actor-observer gap: the same injected error is corrected when attributed to the user but missed when attributed to the model's own output. Appending the word 'Wait' removes most of the gap.
numbers: 14 open-source non-reasoning models; average blind spot 64.5%. 'Wait' prompt cuts the blind spot by 89.3% on average. Fine-tuning on 5,306 error-correction traces cuts it by 76.0%. Datasets: SCLI5, GSM8K-SC, PRM800K-SC.
limits: Injected errors, not natural ones. Cause (training data lacks correction traces) is argued, not proven.
agent_relevance: Strong support for a forced second-look step that treats own output as external. A 'Wait' style cue is cheap.

source: Salemi, Krishnan & Purohit (2026) Debiasing LLMs toward Social Factors in Online Behavior Analytics through Prompt Knowledge Tuning
finding: Llama3, Mistral and Gemma under-use dispositional (user goal) or situational (message context) causes in zero-shot classification. Adding a model-generated goal or context hint as a prompt aid raised macro-F1 on most datasets and beat a Self-Debias baseline.
numbers: Intent (dispositional) Llama3 macro-F1: Lilac 80.8 to 88.7, Thomas 82.5 to 86.2. Theme (situational) Mistral: Alberta 81.0 to 82.8, Colorado 83.6 to 84.8. Multilingual: method best in 8 of 12 model-language cells; Self-Debias lowered Mistral results.
limits: Bias is inferred from the F1 gap on disaster social-media data, not measured directly. Gains smaller for low-resource languages. Not a replication of the classic FAE.
agent_relevance: A two-part prompt (what is the actor's goal; what is the context) helps classification. Supports an operator that elicits person and situation causes separately.

source: Zhou & Di Eugenio (2025) Veracity Bias and Beyond: Uncovering LLMs' Hidden Beliefs in Problem-Solving Reasoning
finding: Five human-value-aligned LLMs attribute correct solutions unevenly across demographic groups and rate identical solutions differently by perceived author.
numbers: Page gives directions only: fewer correct and more incorrect solutions attributed to African-American groups in math and coding; Asian authorship least preferred in writing evaluation; stereotype colours in visualisation code. No numbers read.
limits: Only the abstract page was read, not the paper tables. This is attribution of ability to groups, adjacent to dispositional attribution, not a situational-vs-dispositional test.
agent_relevance: LLM judges attach ability traits to authors. Hide author identity when the agent grades solutions.

source: Search note: no LLM run of the Jones-Harris or culture attribution paradigms was found
finding: arXiv title searches for 'fundamental attribution error' and 'correspondence bias' returned no paper that runs the quiz-game or attitude-attribution task on LLMs. Related LLM work covers demographic attribution bias and self-correction.
numbers: arXiv listing for 'fundamental attribution error': 2 results (2406.13813 chatbots correcting cognitive biases; 1906.09689 robot fallacies). 'correspondence bias': no relevant hits.
limits: Web search budget was exhausted; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex rate limits blocked broader searches. Absence in these searches is not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Gap: an LLM version of Jones-Harris with coin-toss assignment and cross-language prompts would be new and cheap to run.
